UPDATE 2026-09-25 (observed, read-only; supersedes the 2026-09-24 note, which wrongly said this job STILL 401s): the job WORKS. net._http_response at 2026-09-25 00:00:01 shows 200 {"ok":true,"count":13246}, with no 401s in the window. A credential-free GET to refresh-symbols reaches OUR code (405), so verify_jwt is OFF in prod, and `supabase functions download` shows the deployed function is PR #9's original security commit 2dd699f (F5: constant-time apikey guard against SB_SECRET_KEY_CRON). Migration 20260811000000 (applied) supplies the vault cron apikey header, so the two halves of F5 are both live. The REPO is the stale side: main's refresh-symbols has no guard and config.toml says verify_jwt=true, so deploying this function from pre-PR#9 main (including a bare `supabase functions deploy`) would REGRESS it into genuine 401s. Merging PR #9 removes that hazard. CAVEAT for verifying any cron target here: no cron migration sets timeout_milliseconds, so pg_net's 5 s default applies and a target that runs longer shows as a client timeout in net._http_response even on success (enrich-symbols does, every run). This job finishes inside 5 s, so its 200 row is real; for slower targets verify by the data they write.

HISTORY: The oldest job in the schedule (jobid 7, versus 18-21 for the cron-auth-migrated set) and the only one that sends no auth header at all. It predates the RLS-hardening pass that set verify_jwt=true on refresh-symbols, and it was never migrated because no migration in the repo schedules it — it was created out-of-band, so the Phase 2b sweep over supabase/migrations/ never saw it. Its `symbols` target table is likewise created by no migration. IMPORTANT when diagnosing this: cron.job_run_details reports 'succeeded' for every run regardless, because net.http_post is asynchronous — the job status records that the request was ENQUEUED (return_message '1 row' is the request id), not what the server answered. Checked 2026-07-27: five consecutive 'succeeded' runs, which is exactly what a job 401ing every six hours also looks like. Use net._http_response, or check whether the symbols rows actually changed.

nodes.annotation:
~1500 lines, and the only production caller is one cron job. Runs with verify_jwt=false, so the in-code constant-time apikey check is the entire authentication boundary — note it runs before the body parse and before the DB client is constructed, which is what makes an unauthenticated request cheap to reject. The extracted modules (grouping, scoring-eligibility, playoff-progression, job-status) are the parts that have been burned by bugs and are now pinned by hermetic unit tests.

STRANDED STATUS ROWS — FIXED ON BRANCH fix/process-week-results-terminal-status (not yet merged or deployed; prod behaves as described below until it ships). The query-error return now writes 'failed' with the error; the no-pending return writes 'success' with message 'processed 0 matchups: no pending matchups'. The writer lives in job-status.ts (hermetic tests in job-status.test.ts), checks the upsert's resolved { error }, and never throws, so a failed status write cannot change the HTTP response. The CHECK constraint allows only running|success|failed|retrying, so 'nothing to do' vs 'scored something' is carried by the message text, which BOTH success paths always write. A comment at the 'running' write states the invariant: every later handler return writes a terminal status first.

Pre-fix behaviour (traced 2026-07-27; line numbers as of main @ 2be4638): It writes 'running' to cron_job_status at index.ts:880, but terminal statuses exist at only two places: 'success' at :1490 and 'failed' at :1504. Two returns sit between them and write NEITHER, leaving the row permanently at 'running':
  - :919 — no pending matchups. Returns HTTP 200, logs 'No pending matchups to process'. This is the common path.
  - :914 — the matchup query itself failed. Returns HTTP 500, logs 'Error fetching matchups:'.
Discriminate the two by status code or by that log line. The returns before :880 (:848 apikey rejected, :861 missing config) write no row at all, which is a different and less confusing state. :1338 and :1352 are returns inside the nested updateUserStandings helper, not handler returns.

NOT A SCORING OUTAGE. Five consecutive Fridays (2026-06-26 through 07-24) sat at 'running'. `unscored` was confirmed 0 across every league — no matchups with team1_gain IS NULL and week_end < now() — so :919 firing weekly is the function correctly reporting there is nothing to score. Re-confirmed 2026-09-24: the only completed leagues in prod are three old test leagues whose seasons are over. The stranded row is the entire finding. Do not read those five rows as five missed scoring runs.

See CLAUDE.md silent-failure #6 for why this shape is worse than a merely wrong signal.
nodes.label: process-week-results

nodes.annotation:
MODERNISED 2026-07-28 — the last live instance of the partial-state pattern is closed. Decision logic now lives in the pure, hermetically tested close.ts (22 tests), mirroring snapshot-week-start/plan.ts.

THE GUARD IT REPLACED: `alreadyProcessed = existingSnapshots.some(s => s.week_end_price != null)`. ANY single end-priced row marked the WHOLE league-week done, so a run that priced some participants and then threw left a partial write that the retry SKIPPED rather than healed. It also made retries into this function ineffective even after schedule_snapshot_retry was fixed in 20260727000000 — the retry fired and no-opped.

WHY close.ts IS NOT SYMMETRICAL WITH plan.ts, deliberately: week-START has one write path (insert per holding); week-END has TWO, so 'missing' has two kinds. KIND 1 is an existing Monday row whose week_end_price is still NULL (resolve by UPDATE on id). KIND 2 is a mid-week buy with no row at all (resolve by INSERT carrying entered_mid_week=true and the weighted entry price as week_start_price). Completeness is the CONJUNCTION of both, per participant — checking only kind 1 would call a league complete while a mid-week buy went unrecorded.

The coverage gate runs BEFORE the Alpaca call, so a complete league costs no quota. Writes are all-or-nothing: one unpriceable symbol aborts the whole league (buildCloseWork returns empty updates AND inserts alongside missingSymbols, so a careless caller cannot write a subset). Inserts upsert on (league_id,user_id,week_number,symbol), so overlapping retries re-converge. anyIncomplete now forces terminal status 'retrying'/'failed' — a partial run can no longer report 'success'.
nodes.label: snapshot-week-end

nodes.annotation:
Modernised in 2caf9f8: all-or-nothing writes per league-week, with a completeness-based coverage gate that runs BEFORE any Alpaca call and skips on alreadyEndPriced / none_expected / complete, healing only the missing participants when coverage is partial.

READ THE 'will retry' LOG WITH SUSPICION. The ABORT path at index.ts:466 refuses a partial snapshot and logs '... refusing partial snapshot, will retry'. Until 2026-07-27 that promise was never kept: schedule_snapshot_retry passed a TIMESTAMPTZ to cron.schedule, which has no such overload, so it raised on every call and no retry was ever scheduled. FIXED by 20260727000000 (applied; see pg.schedule_snapshot_retry) — an aborted league now re-attempts via a one-shot retry job. Still verify a retry by the 'retrying' row in cron_job_status and the healed week_snapshots rows, not by this log line.

ZERO WRITES IS OFTEN CORRECT. Paths producing no week_snapshots rows: :302 Monday holiday (early return, loop never runs), :324 no active matchup leagues, :357 no matchups for the league-week, :413 already_end_priced, :420 no_holdings, :425 already_complete. The two that indicate a PROBLEM are :466 (abort, unpriced symbols) and :494 (upsert error) — and both set anyIncomplete, which forces status 'retrying' (:516) or 'failed' (:530). So terminal status 'success' at :540 PROVES neither problem path fired. Zero rows plus 'success' means every league hit a benign skip.

One trap in that list: :302 depends on isMarketOpenToday, which returns open:false on a 401 (CLAUDE.md silent-failure #1). A stale Alpaca key therefore produces 'success' + zero rows + the log line 'Monday is a market holiday, skipping' on a day that is not a holiday.

nodes.annotation: The batch key is (league_id, week_number), not league_id. Grouping by league alone meant a league with several unscored weeks scored every one of them against week[0]'s snapshots and trade window. The sort order is equally load-bearing: the handler advances current_week only when the batch's week equals the league's current week, so weeks must arrive ascending or a league gets permanently stuck.

nodes.annotation:
The cron_job_status writer, extracted so its failure handling is pinned by hermetic tests. Two contracts: (1) it destructures the upsert's resolved { error } — supabase-js does not throw on a Postgres error, and the previous inline writer discarded the result, so a rejected status write was invisible; (2) it NEVER throws and returns a boolean, so a failed telemetry write cannot turn the handler's 200 into a 500.

Both success summaries (noPendingMessage / scoredMessage) are always non-empty. That is deliberate: the no-pending and scored paths both write 'success', so if only one wrote a message, error_message's NULL-ness would become a discriminator — the overloaded-NULL shape CLAUDE.md warns about. The text carries the distinction; its presence never does.

nodes.annotation: Pure decision functions — no side effects, no Deno APIs; every logging call and DB write stays in index.ts. The evaluation ORDER inside decideBatchScoring is part of the contract: freshness is checked before the week>1 rule, so a stale week>1 batch reports stale_no_snapshots (the actionable operational cause) rather than the generic reason. Swapping them would silently relabel every stale skip.

nodes.annotation:
FIXED and verified 2026-07-27. For its entire life until then it had never scheduled a retry: it declared retry_time TIMESTAMPTZ and passed it to cron.schedule, which has only (schedule text, command text) and (job_name text, schedule text, command text) overloads — and PostgreSQL removed implicit datetime->text casts in 8.3, so the call resolved to nothing and raised on every invocation.

It survived three migrations looking healthy because PL/pgSQL resolves called-function names at EXECUTION time, not at CREATE FUNCTION time — a migration applying cleanly says nothing about whether its function bodies work. And it left no trace because the INSERT INTO cron_job_status ... 'retrying' sits AFTER the PERFORM and a function body is atomic, so the raise rolled back its own evidence.

The fix passes a five-field cron expression formatted from the retry instant in cron.timezone. Proven live: calling it returned without error (it previously raised) and wrote a 'retrying' row — THE FIRST that table has ever held. That row is the evidence; before the fix the query for it could only ever return zero rows.

Note the change is BEHAVIOR-ADDING. MAX_RETRIES is 3 in both callers and the initial run counts as attempt 1, so a failing run can now re-invoke its function up to 2 more times. For snapshot-week-start that is safe and useful — the coverage gate skips complete leagues and heals only missing participants. For snapshot-week-end it was safe but INEFFECTIVE until 2026-07-28: its old existence-only alreadyProcessed guard skipped a league as soon as ANY row carried a week_end_price. The per-participant coverage gate in close.ts replaced that guard, so week-end retries now heal partial writes too (see fn.snapshot-week-end).

nodes.annotation:
The ops table three cron functions write, with UNIQUE(job_name, run_date) and run_date defaulting to CURRENT_DATE — so each job gets exactly one row per day and every write is an upsert onto it.

Do NOT treat this table as a reliable health signal until the process-week-results fix is DEPLOYED. In prod today, process-week-results writes 'running' and, on its two most likely returns (the matchup-query error and the no-pending-matchups return), never writes a terminal status — so a row reading 'running' is byte-identical whether the function hung, crashed mid-run, or completed normally with nothing to do. Branch fix/process-week-results-terminal-status makes both returns write a terminal status ('failed' / 'success' + 'processed 0 matchups: no pending matchups') and checks each write's resolved { error }. Until that ships, snapshot-week-start and snapshot-week-end are the only jobs whose rows reach a terminal status on every path; note their writers still discard the upsert's { error }, so a REJECTED status write there is still silent. Any alerting built on this table must account for that asymmetry or it will either fire every week or never fire at all.

error_message is the table's only free-text column. On process-week-results 'success' rows it holds a run summary, not an error — read status for the outcome.

Also note the upsert semantics when testing by hand: calling schedule_snapshot_retry directly OVERWRITES the day's real row for that job rather than inserting a new one.

Policy note: `service_role_only` is PUBLIC-role but gates on `auth.role() = 'service_role'`, which IS a real caller check — anon resolves to 'anon' and matches nothing. An earlier version of the generator graded this HIGH because its identity-check heuristic looked only for auth.uid()/auth.jwt()/is_member/is_commissioner and missed auth.role(). Fixed. If a policy here ever shows up as ungated again, check the predicate before believing it.

DROPPED 2026-07-28 (migration 20260728000000). This key is retained deliberately so the decision survives; it will surface as an orphanAnnotation once db-snapshot.json is re-captured, and THAT is the signal the drop reached prod. Remove it then.

WHAT IT WAS: policy "Service role can insert notifications" — the NAME claimed service-role-only, the role list was PUBLIC and the WITH CHECK was literally `true`. Confirmed live via pg_policy (polroles '{-}' = PUBLIC). So any holder of the publishable key, including anon, could INSERT arbitrary rows without limit. The name enforced nothing; only the role list and the predicate do.

AN UNEXPLOITED HOLE, NOT A NEAR-MISS: count(*) was 0 with null min/max sent_at — the table was never written to by anyone, us or otherwise. Record it that way. There is no incident here, and no data to forensically examine; the finding is that the door was open, not that someone walked through it.

WHY DROP RATHER THAN FIX THE PREDICATE: zero readers and zero writers repo-wide (clients, edge functions, plpgsql bodies, cron SQL — independently re-verified by security-reviewer). Its own creating migration (20260122000000) calls it "optional, for debugging/history". Repairing the policy would have left a table with no reader and no writer, so "who inserts into this?" would resurface at every audit. If push-notification logging is wanted later it should return WITH the code that writes it, and with a service_role-scoped policy from the start (see tbl.cron_job_status, whose auth.role() = 'service_role' predicate is the correct shape).

NOT dropped: user_profiles.expo_push_token / notifications_enabled, added by the same migration. Those are LIVE (apps/mobile/lib/notifications.ts) and untouched.

nodes.annotation:
DECIDED 2026-07-28 — KEEP the public SELECT policy. This is settled; do not re-derive it.

The policy is REQUIRED, not merely tolerated. That distinction is the whole point of this note, because the two readings produce the same migration today and opposite futures. symbol-name/index.ts:35 and symbols-search/index.ts:78 both construct their client with SB_PUBLISHABLE_KEY and do NOT forward the caller's Authorization header, so their queries execute as the anon role. The `USING (true)` policy is what makes symbol lookup and search return rows at all. Tighten it to `TO authenticated` — the change that looks obviously safe by analogy with every other table hardened in B1 — and both functions silently return empty: no error, no 401, just a search box that finds nothing.

WHY IT GRADES HIGH ANYWAY: the map's heuristic flags any policy whose predicate contains no identity check. That is the rule working as designed, not a finding. The data is public NASDAQ/NYSE reference listings refreshed from a public feed, the policy is SELECT-only, and writes go through an RLS-bypassing upsert in refresh-symbols using the secret key. There is nothing user-specific in the table to leak.

IF YOU EVER DO WANT IT LOCKED: the prerequisite is switching symbol-name and symbols-search to SB_SECRET_KEY_INTERNAL first, at which point the anon policy becomes genuinely unnecessary and can be dropped. Doing it in the other order breaks search. Judged not worth the moving parts for public ticker data.

nodes.annotation:
GATED to authenticated 2026-07-28 (migration 20260728000001). Decision made; do not re-derive.

WAS: "Anyone can view profiles" FOR SELECT USING (true) with no TO clause, so PUBLIC — confirmed live via pg_policy (polroles '{-}'). anon could read every username, avatar, expo_push_token and notifications_enabled row. NOW: "Authenticated users can view profiles", TO authenticated, USING (true). The insert/update policies (auth.uid() = id) were correct and are untouched.

RESOLVED TOGETHER WITH get_real_user_ids, as it had to be: 20260724000000 revoked anon EXECUTE on that function, whose whole output is which UUIDs are real users — an answer anon could equally obtain by selecting this table. The pair is now consistent UPWARD (both closed) rather than downward.

WHY THE MECHANISM IS SUFFICIENT, and why the function lesson does NOT transfer: functions have exactly ONE gate (EXECUTE), which is why REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC leaving Supabase's default per-role grants intact was a real hole there (see CLAUDE.md). Tables have TWO layers: the default table-level SELECT grant, and RLS policy role-scoping. With RLS enabled, anon keeps its table grant but matches NO policy, so it gets an empty row set — not an error. Same shape as the B1 league tables, whose anon-read test returned [] in prod.

CONSUMER TRACE (why gating broke nothing): preview-league reads profiles via the service_role admin client, so the join-by-code preview is RLS-immune; web APP_PAUSED renders only LandingPage with every other route <Protected>; both signup paths UPSERT after a session exists; all other reads sit in authenticated mobile screens.

HOW THE MAP GRADES THIS NOW (2026-07-30): the SELECT policy appears as a MEDIUM drift row, groupKey authenticated-role-policies-ungated, reading "ANY-AUTHENTICATED READ of every row". It was briefly graded LOW and described as "not an exposure" — the heuristic computed its ungated-predicate check only over PUBLIC-role policies, so moving the SELECT to `authenticated` in 20260728000001 took it out of scope and the all-gated branch then asserted a table-wide claim from the PUBLIC subset alone. Fixing the anon half must not silence the rest; the generator now grades on the PREDICATE first and the role second.

STILL OPEN (L2, escalated by security-reviewer 2026-07-28): expo_push_token remains readable by EVERY authenticated user, not just its owner. That is not merely a metadata leak — apps/mobile/lib/notifications.ts posts to Expo's public push API using the raw token alone, so any authenticated user who reads this table can push arbitrary notifications to any other user. Remediation: split expo_push_token / notifications_enabled into an owner-scoped table (auth.uid() = id) and leave username / avatar on the broadly-readable surface. Merging the gate did NOT close this.

week_start_price is NOT NULL and always has been. Until 2026-07-27 snapshot-week-end tried to insert NULL into it for mid-week purchases, so that insert failed on every run since 2026-01-15 and those positions were silently dropped from scoring — not merely missing a row, but scored wrong, since calculateUserScore drops a mid-week buy with no end price from BOTH totalGain and totalStartValue.

entered_mid_week is now the discriminator. week_start_price on such a row is the purchase entry price, NOT a Monday open. Both scorers key on the flag, never on the price being null — keying on the price would treat the row as a week-start holding and double-count it, because the same buy is already carried in midWeekTrades. The three UI surfaces that multiply quantity * week_start_price for cost basis need no flag: they compute (currentPrice - entryPrice) * quantity, which is correct for both row kinds.

flows.title: Weekly scoring

steps.detail: net.http_post with an apikey header read from vault secret `cron_apikey`.
Job marked running before any work.
Pending matchups: team1_gain IS NULL, week_end in the past, league_type=matchup. The NULL filter is what makes a re-run idempotent.
One batch per (league_id, week_number), sorted week-ascending. Grouping by league alone was the original bug; the sort is load-bearing for week advancement.
Per batch. Presence of any row sets hasSnapshots; any week_end_price sets hasWeekEndPrices.

GUARDS 1 & 2 — decideBatchScoring. A snapshot-less batch is skipped whole: stale_no_snapshots (>72h) or no_snapshots_week_gt_1. Freshness is checked first, and that order is load-bearing for ops labelling.
Mid-week trades inside [weekStart, weekEnd], then a second read bounded to week_end so a post-week sale cannot empty holdings and flip a win to an auto-loss.
Fallback scorer input — only reachable at week 1.
Latest quotes, IEX feed. Failures are swallowed into an empty price map rather than throwing.
GUARD 3a — decideUserScorer picks full | legacy | fallback | unscoreable per user. A snapshot-less user past week 1 is unscoreable: cumulative-from-entry is all-time P/L, not a weekly delta.
GUARD 3b — decideMatchupScoring refuses any matchup containing an unscoreable participant. Byes gate on team1 only. Refused matchups keep team1_gain NULL and stay pending.
Winner written: bye = auto-win, empty portfolio = auto-loss, else dollar gain, tiebreak percent then playoff seed.
Read-then-increment, not transactional and NOT reversible. This irreversibility is the entire reason guards 1-3 refuse rather than fabricate.
current_week re-read per batch and advanced only when the batch IS the current week — so a guard-skipped week blocks advancement instead of being stepped over.
Season end, from playoffs finals or from standings when playoff_teams = 0.

flows.annotation: The most defensive path in the codebase, and the reason it is defensive is that league_standings increments are irreversible. There is no transaction around the read-then-increment and no compensating write, so a fabricated score cannot be undone by re-running. Three guards therefore refuse rather than guess. Read them in order: decideBatchScoring kills a whole snapshot-less league-week; decideUserScorer marks an individual snapshot-less user unscoreable past week 1; decideMatchupScoring refuses any matchup containing one. All three exist because the fallback scorer returns cumulative-from-draft-entry P/L, which is only a valid weekly delta in week 1.

steps.detail: net.http_post with apikey from vault `cron_apikey`.
Pure planning module — decides which league-weeks need snapshotting and what to fetch.
Historical bars for week-start prices.
ALL-OR-NOTHING per league-week with completeness-based skip (fixed in 2caf9f8). A partial price fetch writes nothing rather than a half-week.
Retry scheduling, shared with snapshot-week-end.

flows.title: Week-end snapshot

trigger.detail: pg_cron `snapshot-week-end` — Friday 21:05 UTC, 10 min before scoring

steps.detail: net.http_post with apikey from vault `cron_apikey`. Runs 10 minutes before process-weekly-matchups — that gap is the entire budget for writing week_end_price before scoring reads it.
Friday close prices.

Pure coverage gate (hermetic tests in close.test.ts). Per-participant completeness replaced the old existence-only alreadyProcessed skip, so a partial week-end write is healed on retry instead of read as done. Deliberately NOT symmetrical with week-start/plan.ts: week-end has two write paths (close an existing Monday row; insert a mid-week buy), so "missing" has two kinds.
Writes week_end_price onto existing Monday rows.

Mid-week purchases: positions with no week-start row get one here, carrying a real weighted-average entry price and entered_mid_week = true, upserted on the (league, user, week, symbol) key. This insert had NEVER succeeded before 2026-07-27 — it wrote week_start_price: null against a NOT NULL column, so every mid-week position was silently dropped from scoring. The flag is what stops the row being double-counted as a Monday holding.
Shared retry path.

flows.annotation:
Read this against flow.week-start-snapshot. The asymmetry USED to be that week-end had no extracted module, no tests and an unaudited write path; that was closed on 2026-07-28 (see fn.snapshot-week-end). Both now have a pure decision module with hermetic tests, a completeness-based coverage gate that runs before any Alpaca call, and all-or-nothing per-league writes.

The REMAINING asymmetry is intrinsic and load-bearing, not debt: week-start inserts one row per holding, while week-end must both CLOSE existing Monday rows and INSERT mid-week buys. That is why close.ts models two kinds of 'missing' where plan.ts models one. Do not refactor them into a shared module on the assumption they are the same shape — they are not.

Timing still matters: week-end runs only ten minutes before scoring, so an aborted league has little room to be healed by a retry before process-week-results reads the same rows. The downstream per-user gate (decideUserScorer -> 'unscoreable') remains the required backstop.

Validated by the shared pure module (_shared/draft-validation.ts), filled at the server-fetched price. KNOWN RACE: two concurrent buys can both pass validation — needs an atomic SECURITY DEFINER RPC.

flows.annotation:
Since DR-001 Phase 3 the trade row is written SERVER-SIDE by record-trade, in the same request that validates it; the client-INSERT policy on trades is gone (20260811000002). The old two-actor gap (a real broker order with no DB row, closed after the fact by sync-alpaca-orders) no longer exists — there is no broker order at all, and place-order / sync-alpaca-orders / broker_credentials are deleted. What remains open is the concurrent-buy race inside record-trade (see the step note).

PARTIAL SALES READ AS A BUG BUT ARE NOT ONE. If a position is partly sold during the week, the matchup and dashboard screens show UNREALIZED P/L on the quantity still held at week end, while the scorer additionally settles the REALIZED P/L of the sold portion from midWeekTrades. So a screen and a standings number can legitimately differ after a partial sale, and the screen will read low. This is pre-existing and symmetrical: week-start holdings behave the same way, because their snapshot quantity is Monday's and the UI never consults trades. Not a defect — but it is the first thing a user will report, so recognise it rather than re-investigating.

flows.title: Season reset

trigger.detail: Commissioner taps reset in league settings

steps.detail: Called directly from the client as an authenticated user. EXECUTE is granted to `authenticated`, so the authorization is NOT the grant — it is an INTERNAL commissioner check inside the function body. That gate is the only thing standing between any league member and the four destructive writes below.

GATE 1 — commissioner check: `commissioner_id = auth.uid()::text`. auth.uid() is NULL for anon, so it fails closed. Checked BEFORE the state guard so an unauthorized caller learns nothing about league state.
WRITE 1 — new league_seasons row at MAX(season_number)+1. This is what preserves the old season, so it must succeed before anything is destroyed.
WRITE 2 — every standings row for the league zeroed: wins, losses, ties, points_for, points_against.
WRITE 3 — DESTRUCTIVE: every matchup for the league is deleted outright. History survives only via league_seasons.final_standings, so if WRITE 1 did not capture it, it is gone.
WRITE 4 — league pointed at the new season: current_season_id, season_status=active, current_week=1. All four writes share one implicit transaction, so a failure rolls back the whole reset.

flows.annotation: The only flow where a destructive operation is authorized entirely inside a function body. EXECUTE on start_new_league_season is granted to `authenticated`, so any logged-in user can call it with any league id. Nothing in the grant layer stops a non-commissioner from resetting someone else's league — the internal commissioner check is the whole control. That is deliberate (the client calls it directly, so it must be authenticated-callable), but it means the gate has to be correct, with no defence in depth if it regresses.
